title: The Case for a Slightly Slower First Answer
summary: The first answer in a thread tends to anchor everything after it. Why a short pause with a purpose beats a fast guess, and how to buy that time without going silent.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
A message lands in the team channel: "Can we ship the export feature by Friday?" You've already half typed a reply: "Yeah, should be fine." It's friendly, it's fast, and it might even be right. But you haven't checked whether export still depends on the API change that slipped last sprint. The cursor blinks at the end of the sentence.

This post is about that moment. Answering fast feels helpful, and often it is. When the question is fuzzy, though, the first answer in a thread has a habit of becoming the thing everyone builds on.

First answers stick

Psychologists call this anchoring: the first number or framing you hear pulls later judgments toward it, even when it's irrelevant. Developers aren't immune. Martin Shepperd, Carolyn Mair and Magne Jørgensen ran experiments with 410 professional developers, showing them either a low or a high productivity figure before asking them to estimate their own project's productivity. The anchor had a large effect on the estimates. A workshop on cognitive biases shrank the effect but didn't remove it (An Experimental Evaluation of a De-biasing Intervention for Professional Software Developers).

Now go back to "should be fine." The PM hears Friday. The designer books the review around Friday. Someone mentions Friday to a customer. Researchers who sat in on estimation sessions and interviewed software professionals describe the same drift: estimates turn into commitments with customers, and people pad their numbers to buy back room to work (Matsubara et al., Buying time in software development). A quick answer to a fuzzy question can lock a whole team into the wrong version of the problem.

Pause, but put a time on it

A slower answer doesn't mean disappearing. Silence is worse than a fast guess: people get anxious and still have nothing to plan around. The trick is a short holding reply with a time attached.

A holding reply that works

"Good question. Export still depends on the API change from last sprint, so let me check where that landed. I'll get back to you by 3 p.m. with a yes, a no, or what it would take."

That reply does three jobs: it shows you're on it, it names what you're checking, and it sets a time. Incident teams use the same pattern. PagerDuty's public incident response guide tells subject matter experts who don't know the cause yet to say they're investigating and keep sending regular updates, and has the internal liaison post status to executives roughly every 30 minutes (PagerDuty Incident Response: During an Incident).

Separate what you know from what you guess

This matters most when something is on fire. When production breaks, everyone wants certainty, and a confident fast answer feels reassuring for about ten minutes. If it's wrong, it sends people down the wrong path and the cost climbs quickly. A grounded answer takes a bit longer because it splits things out: here's what we've confirmed, here's our best guess, here's what we don't know yet, here's the next check. It sounds less dramatic. It's far easier to trust.

The pause helps with people, too. Plenty of questions aren't really about information. "When will it be done?" might be protecting a customer promise, a budget or a team that's already tired. Answer only the literal words and you can be accurate and still miss. A short pause gives you room to ask one more question and find out what the other person is trying to protect.

Don't let slow become a hiding place

Slowness only pays off if you come back with more clarity. If the pause turns into procrastination, it creates the same uncertainty it was supposed to reduce, plus a missed promise. So pause with a purpose: read the source, ask one question, check one assumption, compare two options, then reply when you said you would. If the time comes and you still don't know, say so, and say what you're checking next.

Lots of questions deserve a fast answer. "Is staging down?" "Which branch?" "Can you review my PR today?" If you know, answer. The pause is for fuzzy questions, where a wrong first framing gets expensive.

Over time, people pick up the rhythm. Teams stop racing to answer first and start trying to answer usefully, and threads that used to run hot cool down because nobody has to perform certainty they don't have. If you're on the other side, hearing the first quick story after an incident, Wait for the Whole Story Before You Call It covers that half.

Try this week

  • Before answering a fuzzy question, write down the one thing you'd need to check.
  • Send at least one holding reply with a time on it.
  • In your next incident update, mark each line as confirmed, best guess or unknown.
  • When someone asks "when will it be done?", ask what's riding on the date before you give one.

faqs.a: Silence can be. A short holding reply with a time on it ("checking X, back by 3 p.m.") usually lands better than a fast guess that turns out wrong. PagerDuty's public incident guide tells responders who don't know the cause yet to say they're investigating and keep giving regular updates.

faqs.q: What is anchoring, and why does it matter for estimates?
faqs.a: Anchoring is the pull a first number or framing has on later judgments. In experiments with 410 professional developers, seeing a low or high productivity figure first had a large effect on their estimates, and a workshop on biases reduced the effect without removing it. That's why the first estimate in a thread deserves care.

faqs.q: When should I just answer right away?
faqs.a: When the question is clear and you already know the answer: is staging up, which branch, can you review today. Save the pause for fuzzy questions, where a wrong first framing would send the team down the wrong path.
